content:
# Deuteronomy 5 — Disagreement Log
**Chapter:** Deuteronomy 5 (33 verses — the Decalogue)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA
**Total disagreements logged:** 33

---

## V.1 — "called" vs. "summoned"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "And Moshe called to all Yisra'el and said to them" |
| LOGOS | "And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them" |
| PNEUMA | "Moses summoned all Israel and said to them" |
| **SOPHIA** | "And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them" |

**Ruling:** "Summoned" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). The Hebrew *vayiqra* = "and he called," but Moses is convening a formal national assembly; "summoned" carries appropriate ceremonial weight. The narrative *waw* is preserved per EMET/LOGOS.

---

## V.1 — "ordinances" vs. "judgments"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "the statutes and the ordinances" |
| LOGOS | "the statutes and the judgments" |
| PNEUMA | "the statutes and the ordinances" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the statutes and the ordinances" |

**Ruling:** "Ordinances" (EMET/PNEUMA). Hebrew *mishpatim* in Deuteronomic legal context = ordinances. "Judgments" (LOGOS) implies narrowly judicial verdicts. Consistent with the established ruling in Deuteronomy 4.

---

## V.2 — "cut a covenant" vs. "made a covenant"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "cut with us a covenant at Horeb" |
| LOGOS | "made a covenant with us at Horeb" |
| PNEUMA | "made a covenant with us at Horeb" |
| **SOPHIA** | "made a covenant with us at Horeb" |

**Ruling:** "Made a covenant" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). The Hebrew idiom *karat berit* = "cut a covenant" (from the ratification rite of cutting animals, cf. Gen 15). EMET preserves the etymological image; LOGOS/PNEUMA use the standard English equivalent. SOPHIA adopts "made" for natural English flow while noting the underlying idiom.

---

## V.5 — "afraid because of" vs. "afraid of" the fire

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "for you were afraid of the fire and did not go up" |
| LOGOS | "for you were afraid because of the fire and did not go up" |
| PNEUMA | "because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up" |
| **SOPHIA** | "for you were afraid of the fire and did not go up" |

**Ruling:** "Afraid of the fire" (EMET). The Hebrew *ki yere'tem mip-penei ha-esh* = "for you feared from before the fire." EMET's terse rendering is most direct. LOGOS's "because of" adds a preposition; PNEUMA's "would not" shifts the sense toward refusal rather than fear-induced inability.

---

## V.6 — "house of slaves" vs. "house of slavery"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "out of the house of slaves" |
| LOGOS | "out of the house of slavery" |
| PNEUMA | "out of the place of slavery" |
| **SOPHIA** | "out of the house of slavery" |

**Ruling:** "House of slavery" (LOGOS). The Hebrew *beit avadim* = "house of slaves/slavery." "Slavery" (LOGOS) refers to the condition Egypt imposed; "slaves" (EMET) could imply a house owned by enslaved people. PNEUMA's "place of slavery" replaces *beit* (house) with a vaguer term — rejected. Consistent with Deut 4.

---

## V.7 — "before my face" vs. "before me"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "You shall have no other gods before my face" |
| LOGOS | "You shall have no other gods before me" |
| PNEUMA | "You shall have no other gods before me" |
| **SOPHIA** | "You shall have no other gods before me" |

**Ruling:** "Before me" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). The Hebrew *al panay* = "before my face/presence." EMET's "before my face" is etymologically precise but "before me" is the established English form that preserves the directional/relational meaning without sounding odd.

---

## V.8 — "any form" vs. "any likeness" / "idol" vs. "carved image"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a carved image — any form that is in the heavens" |
| LOGOS | "a carved image — any likeness of what is in the heavens" |
| PNEUMA | "an idol — any carved image of anything in the heaven" |
| **SOPHIA** | "a carved image — any likeness of what is in the heavens" |

**Ruling:** "Carved image — any likeness" (LOGOS). The Hebrew *pesel...temunah* — *pesel* = carved/sculpted image; *temunah* = form, likeness. EMET's "form" is accurate but "likeness" is more standard for *temunah*. PNEUMA restructures the two terms as "idol — any carved image," inverting their order and replacing *pesel* with a looser term; rejected.

---

## V.9 — "upon sons" vs. "upon the children"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "visiting the iniquity of fathers upon sons" |
| LOGOS | "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" |
| PNEUMA | "visiting the guilt of the parents on the children" |
| **SOPHIA** | "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" |

**Ruling:** "The fathers...upon the children" (LOGOS). Hebrew *avot...banim* — *banim* can mean sons or children. "Children" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is preferred as the generational curse applies to all offspring. PNEUMA's "guilt" for *avon* (iniquity) is weaker; "parents" for *avot* (fathers) is a modern gender accommodation not in the Hebrew.

---

## V.9 — "those who hate me" vs. "those who reject me"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "those who hate me" |
| LOGOS | "those who hate me" |
| PNEUMA | "those who reject me" |
| **SOPHIA** | "those who hate me" |

**Ruling:** "Those who hate me" (EMET/LOGOS). Hebrew *sone'ay* = those who hate. *Sane'* is the standard word for hatred. PNEUMA's "reject" softens the relational intensity of the term.

---

## V.10 — "to thousands" vs. "to the thousandth generation"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "showing covenant-faithfulness to thousands, to those who love me" |
| LOGOS | "showing covenant-faithfulness to thousands of those who love me" |
| PNEUMA | "showing covenant-faithfulness to the thousandth generation of those who love me" |
| **SOPHIA** | "showing covenant-faithfulness to thousands — to those who love me" |

**Ruling:** "To thousands" with a clarifying dash (EMET/LOGOS base). The Hebrew *la-alaphim* = "to thousands" — a collective plural without specifying "generations." PNEUMA's "thousandth generation" is a common interpretive tradition but goes beyond the MT. SOPHIA uses a dash to separate the appositive clause more clearly than LOGOS's "of."

---

## V.11 — *shav'* — "to emptiness" vs. "in a vain and destructive way" vs. "misuse"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "You shall not lift up the name of the LORD your God to emptiness [la-shav']" |
| LOGOS | "You shall not take up the name of the LORD your God in a vain and destructive way" |
| PNEUMA | "You shall not misuse the name of the LORD your God" |
| **SOPHIA** | "You shall not lift up the name of the LORD your God to emptiness" |

**Ruling:** "To emptiness" (EMET). Hebrew *la-shav'* = to emptiness/vanity/nothingness — covers false oaths, magical invocations, and frivolous use of the divine name. EMET preserves the semantic range without narrowing. LOGOS's addition of "destructive" imports a connotation (*shav'* does not mean destruction in this context); rejected. PNEUMA's "misuse" is too vague and loses the theological weight of *shav'*.

---

## V.12 — *shamor* — "Keep" vs. "Observe"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "Keep the Shabbat day to sanctify it" |
| LOGOS | "Observe the Sabbath day to keep it holy" |
| PNEUMA | "Keep the Sabbath day holy" |
| **SOPHIA** | "Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it" |

**Ruling:** "Keep...to sanctify it" (EMET structure, SOPHIA's English form). Hebrew *shamor...le-qadsho* = "keep/guard...to make holy." EMET preserves the infinitive purpose clause (*le-qadsho* = to sanctify it). LOGOS uses "keep it holy" which collapses the purpose clause into an adverb; PNEUMA similarly compresses. SOPHIA: "Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it" preserves the purpose clause while using standard English.

---

## V.14 — "male servant / female servant" vs. "male slave / female slave"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "your male servant, and your female servant" |
| LOGOS | "your male slave or your female slave" |
| PNEUMA | "your male or female servant" |
| **SOPHIA** | "your male servant or your female servant" |

**Ruling:** "Male servant / female servant" (EMET/PNEUMA). Hebrew *eved / amah* = servant/slave. The project uses "servant" for *eved* in household contexts throughout (established in Genesis/Leviticus). LOGOS's "slave" is historically accurate but inconsistent with the project convention.

---

## V.14 — "as you do" vs. "as you rest" vs. "as well as you"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "may rest as [you rest]" |
| LOGOS | "may rest as well as you" |
| PNEUMA | "may rest just as you do" |
| **SOPHIA** | "may rest as you do" |

**Ruling:** "As you do" (PNEUMA base, without "just"). Hebrew *kamokha* = "like you." EMET's bracketed addition is explanatory but unnecessary; LOGOS's "as well as" introduces a concessive nuance absent from *kamokha*; PNEUMA's "just as you do" is close; SOPHIA simplifies to "as you do."

---

## V.15 — "a strong hand" vs. "a mighty hand"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm" |
| LOGOS | "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" |
| PNEUMA | "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" |
| **SOPHIA** | "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" |

**Ruling:** "A strong hand" (EMET). Hebrew *yad chazaqah* — *chazaq* = strong/firm. Consistent ruling throughout Deuteronomy; *chazaq* ≠ *gibor* (mighty). See Deut 4 ruling.

---

## V.15 — "to keep the Sabbath day" vs. "to do the Sabbath day"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "to do the Shabbat day" |
| LOGOS | "to keep the Sabbath day" |
| PNEUMA | "to keep the Sabbath day" |
| **SOPHIA** | "to keep the Sabbath day" |

**Ruling:** "To keep the Sabbath day" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). Hebrew *la'asot et-yom ha-Shabbat* = "to do/observe the Sabbath day." In English the idiom "keep the Sabbath" is the established form; "do the Sabbath day" (EMET) is a wooden rendering of *la'asot*.

---

## V.16 — "so that your days may be long" vs. "so that your days may be lengthened"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "so that your days may be lengthened" |
| LOGOS | "so that your days may be long" |
| PNEUMA | "so that you will live long" |
| **SOPHIA** | "so that your days may be long" |

**Ruling:** "So that your days may be long" (LOGOS). Hebrew *le-ma'an ya'arikun yamekha* = "so that your days may be lengthened." LOGOS's "long" is a natural English equivalent; EMET's "lengthened" is more literal but less idiomatic; PNEUMA's "live long" loses the "days" image central to the Hebrew idiom.

---

## V.16 — "in the land" vs. "upon the soil"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "upon the soil that the LORD your God is giving to you" |
| LOGOS | "in the land that the LORD your God is giving you" |
| PNEUMA | "in the land the LORD your God is giving you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "in the land that the LORD your God is giving you" |

**Ruling:** "In the land" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). The Hebrew *ha-adamah* = ground/soil/land. EMET: "upon the soil" is literal for *adamah* (differentiated from *eretz* = land); however, in this promise context "in the land" is the natural English idiom, and the subtle *adamah/eretz* distinction is better addressed in notes than in translation. SOPHIA follows the natural rendering.

---

## V.20 — *ed shav'* — "a lying witness" vs. "a witness of falsehood" vs. "false testimony"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a witness of falsehood [ed shav']" |
| LOGOS | "with a false witness" |
| PNEUMA | "false testimony against your neighbor" |
| **SOPHIA** | "as a lying witness" |

**Ruling:** "A lying witness" (SOPHIA original). Hebrew *ed shav'* = a witness of *shav'* (emptiness/falsehood). EMET's "witness of falsehood" is accurate but awkward; LOGOS's "false witness" is clean but loses the *shav'* vs. *shaqer* distinction; PNEUMA's "false testimony" shifts from witness-as-person to the content of the testimony — rejected. SOPHIA: "lying witness" preserves the personal noun while rendering *shav'* functionally.

---

## V.21 — two-verb coveting commandment

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "you shall not covet...you shall not desire" |
| LOGOS | "you shall not covet...you shall not desire" |
| PNEUMA | "You shall not covet...You shall not crave" |
| **SOPHIA** | "you shall not covet...you shall not desire" |

**Ruling:** "Covet...desire" (EMET/LOGOS). Hebrew *lo tachmod* (covet/desire possessively) for the wife; *lo tit'aveh* (desire/crave) for house and property. The two-verb distinction must be preserved; PNEUMA's "crave" for *tit'aveh* is accurate but SOPHIA prefers "desire" as more natural and less colloquial. The structural split between wife (first clause) and property (second clause) is maintained.

---

## V.21 — "his field" — present in Deuteronomy, absent from Exodus 20

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "your neighbor's house, his field, and his male servant" |
| LOGOS | "your neighbor's house, his field, or his male slave" |
| PNEUMA | "your neighbor's house, or his field, or his male or female servant" |
| **SOPHIA** | "your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant" |

**Ruling:** All three include "field," consistent with the MT of Deuteronomy 5:21, which adds *sadeh* (field) to the list — a term absent from the parallel Exodus 20:17. SOPHIA preserves the Deuteronomic expansion.

---

## V.22 — "he added nothing more" vs. "he added not"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a great voice and he added not [to it]" |
| LOGOS | "a great voice — and he added nothing more" |
| PNEUMA | "with a great voice. He added nothing more." |
| **SOPHIA** | "a great voice — and he added nothing more" |

**Ruling:** "He added nothing more" with em-dash continuation (LOGOS). EMET's bracketed addition is interpretive and the "added not" construction is archaic; PNEUMA breaks the sentence, separating the *ve-lo yasaf* clause into its own sentence — this gives it more weight but slightly disrupts the participial flow of the Hebrew. LOGOS's dash-continuation is preferred.

---

## V.22 — "entire assembly" vs. "all your assembly"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "to all your assembly" |
| LOGOS | "to your entire assembly" |
| PNEUMA | "to your whole assembly" |
| **SOPHIA** | "to your entire assembly" |

**Ruling:** "Your entire assembly" (LOGOS). "Entire" captures *kol* in context of a comprehensive formal gathering; "all your assembly" (EMET) is slightly redundant; "whole assembly" (PNEUMA) is acceptable but SOPHIA follows LOGOS for consistency.

---

## V.24 — "and he lives" vs. "man still lives"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "God speaks with man and he lives" |
| LOGOS | "God speaks with man and man still lives" |
| PNEUMA | "God can speak with a person and the person still lives" |
| **SOPHIA** | "God speaks with man and man still lives" |

**Ruling:** "Man still lives" (LOGOS). EMET's "he lives" leaves an ambiguous pronoun (does "he" refer to God or man?). LOGOS's repetition of "man" resolves the ambiguity. PNEUMA's "can speak" introduces a modal of capability that softens the declarative force; "person" for *ha-adam* (man/human) is acceptable but inconsistent with the project's gendered usage in this formula.

---

## V.25 — "if we go on hearing" vs. "if we continue hearing" vs. "if we hear any more"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "if we continue hearing the voice of the LORD our God any more" |
| LOGOS | "if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more" |
| PNEUMA | "If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer" |
| **SOPHIA** | "if we go on hearing the voice of the LORD our God any more" |

**Ruling:** "If we go on hearing...any more" (SOPHIA hybrid). Hebrew *im yosifim anachnu lishmo'a* = "if we continue/add to hearing." EMET's "continue" is accurate; LOGOS drops the continuative idea; PNEUMA's "any longer" is close. SOPHIA: "go on hearing" preserves the continuative sense of *yasaf* (to add/continue) while flowing naturally.

---

## V.28 — "They have done well" vs. "All that they have spoken is good" vs. "Everything they said is good"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "They have done well [in] all that they have spoken" |
| LOGOS | "All that they have spoken is good" |
| PNEUMA | "Everything they said is good" |
| **SOPHIA** | "They have spoken well in all that they have said" |

**Ruling:** SOPHIA original ("They have spoken well"). The Hebrew *hetivo kol asher diberu* = "they have done well / rightly — all that they have spoken." EMET preserves the verbal commendation (*hetivo*); LOGOS/PNEUMA nominalize ("is good"), which is grammatically possible but loses the commendation verb. SOPHIA: "They have spoken well" integrates *hetivo* as an adverb on *diberu*, which is natural and preserves the divine approval language.

---

## V.29 — divine optative — "O that" vs. "Oh that" vs. "If only"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "O that there were in their heart such a heart as this" |
| LOGOS | "Oh, that their heart were like this" |
| PNEUMA | "If only their hearts would be inclined to fear me" |
| **SOPHIA** | "O that there were in them such a heart as this" |

**Ruling:** "O that there were in them such a heart as this" (EMET base, modified). Hebrew *mi-yitten ve-hayah levavam zeh lahem* = "who will give that this heart were in them" — the Hebrew optative formula expressing a wish. EMET's "O that" is the most formally appropriate English optative. LOGOS's "Oh that their heart were like this" loses the existential image of the heart *being in* them. PNEUMA's "inclined to fear me" adds "inclined" which is not in the Hebrew. SOPHIA adopts EMET's structure, replacing "in their heart such a heart as this" with "in them such a heart as this" for natural English flow.

---

## V.31 — "commandments and the statutes and the ordinances" vs. "judgments"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "the commandment and the statutes and the ordinances" |
| LOGOS | "the commandments and the statutes and the judgments" |
| PNEUMA | "the commandments, statutes, and ordinances" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the commandments and the statutes and the ordinances" |

**Ruling:** "Commandments...statutes...ordinances" (EMET/PNEUMA, pluralized). Hebrew *ha-mitsvah...ha-chuqqim...ha-mishpatim* — the full Deuteronomic legal triad. EMET uses the singular *ha-mitsvah* (the commandment) for the collective, which is grammatically accurate but unclear in English; pluralized. "Judgments" (LOGOS) rejected per the standing ruling on *mishpatim*.

---

## V.32 — "take care to do" vs. "be careful to do" vs. "So you shall take care"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "And you shall take heed to do as the LORD your God commanded you" |
| LOGOS | "So you shall take care to do as the LORD your God has commanded you" |
| PNEUMA | "So be careful to do what the LORD your God has commanded you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "And you shall take care to do as the LORD your God commanded you" |

**Ruling:** "Take care to do" (LOGOS base). Hebrew *u-shmartem la'asot* = "and you shall keep/guard to do." "Take care" (LOGOS) is natural; EMET's "take heed" is slightly archaic; PNEUMA's "be careful" is acceptable but weaker. SOPHIA: preserves the narrative *waw* (EMET/LOGOS) rather than PNEUMA's "So."

---

## V.33 — "prolong your days" vs. "lengthen days" vs. "live long"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "you may lengthen days in the land" |
| LOGOS | "that you may prolong your days in the land" |
| PNEUMA | "you will live long in the land" |
| **SOPHIA** | "you may prolong your days in the land" |

**Ruling:** "Prolong your days" (LOGOS). Hebrew *le-ha'arikun yamim* = "to lengthen days." LOGOS's "prolong your days" is the standard English idiom; EMET's "lengthen days" is direct but less natural; PNEUMA's "live long" loses the "days" image.
